Publisher XML converted to located text (jats_text): abstract and figure/table captions only
pages_convention: XML section and paragraph locators (jats_text) where the XML holds the text (abstract §0 ¶1 and figure captions); the supplied XML contains no body paragraphs, so body text is cited by printed journal pages (identical to PDF pages counted from 1); figure-content steps cite the figure label as printed with the PDF page

entry.evidence: the effect of water on olivine dislocation creep must be examined using a method that is independent of deformation and diffusion techniques

sequences.source_document: Published paper (PDF) with publisher XML abstract and captions

steps.action: Authors take from earlier deformation experiments the claim that water strongly enhances olivine dislocation creep (exponent about 1.2) and induces fabric transitions.
steps.quote: suggested that water incorporation strongly enhances olivine dislocation creep

steps.action: Authors set against it the rival from Si and O diffusion studies: water has a small, orientation-independent effect, so a fabric transition is unlikely.
steps.quote: showed a small effect of water incorporation

steps.action: Authors argue that both prior approaches rest on problematic assumptions or conditions and pose the question of the water effect with an independent method.
steps.quote: the effect of water on olivine dislocation creep must be examined using a method that is independent of deformation and diffusion techniques

steps.action: Authors design the test with the dislocation recovery method, choosing a-slip and c-slip as the least and most water-sensitive slip systems and excluding [100](001) and [001](010).
steps.quote: we adopted the dislocation recovery method

steps.action: From the polycrystal exponent of 1.2, authors derive the expectation that the a-dislocation exponent lies below 1.2 and the c-dislocation exponent above it.
steps.quote: We therefore expect that the water-content exponent of the a- and c-dislocations may be lower and higher than 1.2, respectively.

steps.action: Authors set laboratory conditions: they hydrate or dehydrate oriented crystals to 5–800 wt. ppm, shear them at 5 GPa and 1470 K to activate a- or c-dislocations, cut them into paired pieces, and anneal at 5 GPa and 1473 K.
steps.quote: Natural olivine single crystals were doped with 5–800 wt. ppm water and sheared in the [100] or [001] directions

steps.action: Authors measure water contents by FTIR (Paterson calibration) before and after annealing and find them nearly unchanged and below olivine water solubility.
steps.quote: Despite annealing, the water contents remained nearly unchanged

steps.action: Authors check water homogeneity by comparing FTIR spectra from rims and centers of annealed hydrous samples.
steps.quote: The spectra measured at the rims and centers of the hydrated annealed samples were identical.

steps.action: Authors image dislocations by oxidation decoration (SEM) and TEM; dominant c-dislocation segments switch from screw to edge near 25 wt. ppm, while a-dislocations stay edge-dominated.
steps.quote: The TEM images show that screw segments of the c-dislocations dominate (Fig. 4A) at lower water contents (<25 wt. ppm)

steps.action: Authors run a cold-compression control without heating to verify that the observed dislocations formed during high-temperature deformation.
steps.quote: No dislocations were observed in the cold compressed sample after oxidation decoration treatment

steps.action: Authors compute k from dislocation densities of the rate-limiting segments via Eq. (2), omitting annealing-generated dislocations as negligible, and fit k to a power law in water content.
steps.quote: The obtained annihilation rate coefficients are fitted to a power-law equation, yielding astonishingly small water-content exponents of 0.0 ± 0.1 and 0.2 ± 0.2

steps.action: Authors check the second-order kinetics premise of Eq. (1) by showing k does not depend on the initial dislocation density.
steps.quote: Our calculated k is independent of the initial dislocation density, which indicates that the recovery follows second-order kinetics.

steps.action: Authors compare the fitted exponents with the stated expectation: both are far below 1.2 and identical within error.
steps.quote: [...] to these expectations, our results demonstrate that the water-content exponents of the a- and c-dislocations are substantially smaller

steps.action: Authors qualify the c-slip exponent: it may be higher below 25 wt. ppm where screw segments limit mobility and more uncertain given the 1.3-order water range, but they argue edge-limited mobility governs typical mantle water contents.
steps.quote: Therefore, c-dislocations may have a higher water-content exponent than the current estimation

steps.action: Authors compare with polycrystalline deformation exponents (1.2) and recompute those with a 2.5 cm3/mol activation volume (giving 0.7 and 0.5), which remain higher; differences in oxygen fugacity and Si activity are ruled out as the cause.
steps.quote: The water-content exponents obtained in this study are considerably smaller than those suggested by early polycrystalline-olivine deformation experiments

steps.action: Authors propose, without testing, two explanations for the discrepancy: a pressure-dependent water exponent, and grain-boundary migration or sliding enhanced by free water in water-saturated experiments.
steps.quote: One possibility is that the water-content exponent is pressure dependent.

steps.action: Authors compare with single-crystal deformation studies (Mackwell 1985, Girard 2013, Tielke 2017, 2019), which give exponents of about 0 to 0.4, consistent with theirs.
steps.quote: Our results generally agree with single-crystal deformation results

steps.action: Authors extrapolate k to asthenospheric conditions along a 70-Ma geotherm, using cited activation energy and volumes, and compute a- and c-slip viscosities at 5 and 1000 wt. ppm water.
steps.quote: The viscosity was calculated using Eq. (2) with k extrapolated from the present study.

steps.action: Authors keep the claim that water lowers asthenospheric viscosity by less than half an order of magnitude, so the lithosphere-asthenosphere contrast is mainly thermal.
steps.quote: A strong viscosity contrast between the lithosphere and asthenosphere is therefore difficult to produce from a difference in water content alone

steps.action: Because the computed ηa and ηc do not cross over, authors reject the water-induced A- to C-type fabric transition in the oceanic asthenosphere.
steps.quote: The present results suggest that a water-induced A- to C-type fabric transition (Karato et al., 2008) may not occur in the oceanic asthenosphere.

steps.action: Authors reinterpret lateral seismic anisotropy variations (e.g., VSV > VSH under Iceland and Hawaii) as reflecting flow geometry such as plume upwelling.
steps.quote: the lateral seismic anisotropy changes observed in the asthenosphere may solely reflect changes of mantle flow geometry

steps.action: Authors conclude that water exponents are small for both slip systems, that the aggregate exponent is below 0.4, that creep enhancement is negligible and a fabric transition unlikely, and that the c-slip exponent needs a wider water range.
steps.quote: These results imply that water incorporation does not effectively increase the dislocation-creep rate and that a water-induced fabric transition is unlikely.

tree.answer: Water effect on olivine dislocation creep, claimed by prior deformation work and disputed by diffusion work
No; dislocation mobility inferred through the annihilation rate coefficient k
Constrain the water-content exponent of dislocation mobility for a- and c-slip
Strong, slip-system-dependent enhancement (r near 1.2) versus small, uniform effect (diffusion studies)
Yes: a below and c above 1.2, versus small similar exponents
Set in the laboratory: water content, P, T and slip system controlled in a multi-anvil press
Partly: cold-compression, FTIR homogeneity and initial-density checks pass; c-slip exponent limited by narrow water range
Exponents 0.0 ± 0.1 and 0.2 ± 0.2; strong creep enhancement and water-induced fabric transition judged unlikely

end.claim: Water-content exponents of dislocation mobility are 0.0 ± 0.1 for [100](010) and 0.2 ± 0.2 for [001](100) in olivine at 5 GPa and 1473 K, so water has a small effect on dislocation creep.

decisive_move.sentence: Without fitting the annealing-derived k values against water content to obtain the exponents r, there would be no claim of a small water effect or of an unlikely fabric transition.

gates.evidence: Slip systems were chosen because Jung and Karato (2001) imply they are the least and most water-sensitive, and an expectation (a below, c above 1.2) is stated in the Introduction (p. 2). The fitted exponents could have matched or exceeded 1.2. Nothing shows the expectation was fixed before the data were seen, and no analysis plan is reported.

imports.item: Dislocation recovery (second-order annihilation) kinetics and climb-controlled dislocation mobility
Transmission electron microscopy with weak-beam dark-field imaging and g·b diffraction contrast
Laser-ablation ICP-MS and FTIR spectroscopy for composition and hydroxyl content

limits: The supplied XML holds only the abstract and captions, so body locators are printed pages. No review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. The paper makes no explicit priority ('first') claim. The rival accounts are framed implicitly as prior literature rather than as formal competing hypotheses; strong_inference is chosen because one measurement (the exponents for two slip systems) discriminates between them, though independent_replication (an independent method re-examining a published effect) is a defensible alternative, by inference. Sub-claims at other statuses: aggregate exponent below 0.4 and viscosity contrast mainly thermal (best_explanation, relying on cited assumptions about aggregate strength and activation volumes); water-induced A- to C-type fabric transition unlikely (best_explanation from extrapolated viscosities with no crossover); seismic anisotropy variations caused by flow geometry (untested interpretation); c-slip exponent below 25 wt. ppm may be higher (acknowledged uncertainty). The pressure-dependent exponent and free-water explanations for the discrepancy with polycrystal experiments are not tested. Only one P-T condition was studied, and the replicate pieces ('-2' samples) come from the same deformed crystals. Supplementary tables and figures were not supplied and could not be checked.

disagreements.target: Early polycrystalline-olivine deformation experiments (Mei and Kohlstedt, 2000; Karato and Jung, 2003), water-content exponent 1.2
disagreements.support: Annealing-derived exponents of 0.0 and 0.2 are far below 1.2, and recomputing the earlier exponents with a smaller activation volume still leaves them higher.
disagreements.quote: The water-content exponents obtained in this study are considerably smaller than those suggested by early polycrystalline-olivine deformation experiments (1.2)

disagreements.target: Water-induced A- to C-type olivine fabric transition (Jung and Karato, 2001; Karato et al., 2008)
disagreements.support: Similar exponents for a- and c-slip and no crossover between the extrapolated ηa and ηc imply that A-type fabric dominates.
disagreements.quote: a water-induced A- to C-type fabric transition (Karato et al., 2008) may not occur in the oceanic asthenosphere

disagreements.target: Water-induced lithosphere-asthenosphere viscosity contrast (Hirth and Kohlstedt, 2003; Kohlstedt, 2006)
disagreements.support: Extrapolated viscosities change by only a factor of about three between 5 and 1000 wt. ppm water.
disagreements.quote: A strong viscosity contrast between the lithosphere and asthenosphere is therefore difficult to produce from a difference in water content alone

disagreements.target: Creep rates inferred from Si and O diffusion (Fei et al., 2013, 2014)
disagreements.support: The authors agree with the small effect but argue the diffusion-based inference rests on an assumption that diffusion purely controls creep and uses dislocation-free crystals.
disagreements.quote: This rough assumption hinders any definitive conclusion regarding water effects on the dislocation creep rate and fabric transition.

disagreements.target: Hydrous deformation experiments under water-saturated, high-stress conditions
disagreements.support: The authors argue that the high stresses and water saturation of those experiments are unlike the asthenosphere and confound water and pressure effects.
disagreements.quote: Previous studies therefore could not separate the water effect from the pressure effect, which is poorly understood.

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Deformation experiments; Si and O diffusion measurements
alternatives_considered.reason: Independent of both; applies at low stress and water-undersaturated conditions; slip-system specific
[100](001) is intermediate in water sensitivity; [001](010) appears only above about 400 MPa

alternatives_considered.chosen: Densities of the dominant (rate-limiting) dislocation segments only
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Sum of apparent densities in both directions normal to the slip plane
alternatives_considered.reason: Dominant segments have lower mobility and limit creep; non-dominant density change is negligibly small

alternatives_considered.chosen: Omit dislocations newly produced during annealing
alternatives_considered.reason: Their density is below 0.003 μm−2 (Rubie et al., 1993), negligible relative to final densities

alternatives_considered.chosen: Activation volume of 2.5 cm3/mol (Wang et al., 2017) to recompute literature exponents
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Activation volumes of 34 and 14 cm3/mol used by Mei and Kohlstedt (2000) and Karato and Jung (2003)
alternatives_considered.reason: Large assumed activation volume may explain the high earlier exponents

alternatives_considered.chosen: Aggregate viscosity exponent bounded between ηa and ηc (−0.1 to 0.4)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Aggregate controlled by the strongest slip system, so r = 0.2 ± 0.2
alternatives_considered.reason: Ashby and Duval (1985) suggest strongest-system control at large strain
